title: Three daily checks
hookLine: Zengzi examines himself three times daily: was I loyal, trustworthy, did I practice what I was taught? (Analects 1.4)

cards: If you could check only three things about your day before you slept, which three would you choose? Not your steps or your screen time. Three questions about who you were today.
It's harder than it sounds. A list of ten is easy; ten lets you hide. Three makes you decide what actually matters.
A student of Confucius named Zengzi made that choice, and his answer sits in the opening pages of the Analects, the book of Confucius's sayings. It's short enough to fit on a sticky note.

teach.h: WAS I FAITHFUL IN WORK FOR OTHERS?
teach.b: Here is Zengzi, in James Legge's translation: "I daily examine myself on three points." In plain words: First, in working for someone else, was I faithful? Did I give their task real effort, as if it were my own?

teach.h: WAS I TRUE TO MY FRIENDS?
teach.b: Second, with my friends, was I true to my word?

teach.h: DID I PRACTICE WHAT I WAS TAUGHT?
teach.b: Third, what my teacher passed on to me, did I actually practice it? Look at what's missing. Nothing about success.

Nothing about how others treated me. Nothing about feelings, or luck. All three are about the gap between what I owe and what I did, starting with the self, at close range, with the people right in front of you.
And notice the word daily. Not once a year at a big turning point. Every day, small and plain, like brushing your teeth.
There's a lovely puzzle in the third question.

teach.h: READ TWO WAYS: STUDENT OR TEACHER.
teach.b: The Chinese is so compact it can be read two ways. Some readers take it as: did I practice what was passed on to me?

teach.h: I DAILY EXAMINE MYSELF ON THREE POINTS.
teach.b: Others: did I pass on to others anything I hadn't practiced myself? One is about the student, the other about the teacher, and one person can be both. Either way, the check is the same: do my words and my life match?
The questions don't ask for guilt. They ask for honesty. Zengzi doesn't say what he does with the answers.
Maybe that's the point: the checking itself is the practice.

how: People drawn to Confucian practice use Zengzi's three questions as a daily self-examination, often at the end of the day, sometimes keeping a journal of the answers.

games.q: you're choosing three questions to ask yourself every night. which set is closest to Zengzi's?
o: did I win, did I earn, did I get noticed?

games.why: Zengzi checks faithfulness in work for others, truth with friends, and practicing what he was taught: all about what he owed.

practice: Think back over yesterday, or today so far, and let one moment come up for each question. Did I give real effort to something done for someone else? With a friend, was I true to my word?
Something I've learned, maybe on this path, did I live it even once? Just notice the answers, no scolding, and if you pray, bring what you found into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Three daily checks. Zengzi's questions in the Analects: was I faithful, was I true to my word, did I practice what I was taught. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, from Analects 1.4: three examinations of oneself.
